title: Placental Pathology

paragraphs.text: 25 Placental Pathology
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The placenta has two opposing functions. It is the sole source of sustenance for the fetus and its sole protection against noxious external influences. It can be argued that no evaluation of a sick neonate is complete without knowing the status of the organ that has accompanied it through the preceding gestation. The specific “value added” by placental examination can be summarized under five overlapping headings: 1. Identification of immediately treatable processes: for
paragraphs.heading: RAYMOND W. REDLINE

paragraphs.text: example, elevated risk of neonatal sepsis (histologic chorioamnionitis with fetal inflammatory response), specific infections (cytomegalovirus [CMV], Candida, syphilis, Listeria, SARS-CoV2), retained placenta, metabolic storage diseases, placental malignancies 2. Determination of the underlying cause of adverse out-
paragraphs.heading: RAYMOND W. REDLINE

paragraphs.text: comes: subclassification of preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction (FGR), and stillbirth into pathophysiologically homogeneous phenotypes 3. Estimation of recurrence risk: different patterns of pla-
paragraphs.heading: RAYMOND W. REDLINE

paragraphs.text: cental injury have distinct and widely disparate rates of recurrence varying from 0% to 70% 4. Guidance for future care path(s): may prompt screening for
paragraphs.heading: RAYMOND W. REDLINE

paragraphs.text: underlying maternal disease and/or genetic testing, high-risk referral, enhanced antenatal surveillance, initiation of antenatal therapy, elective early delivery in future pregnancies 5. Quality assurance and risk management: gold standard
paragraphs.heading: RAYMOND W. REDLINE

paragraphs.text: distinguishing true and false-positive and negative clinical diagnoses (e.g., chorioamnionitis, abruption); identifies subacute and chronic disorders predisposing to neonatal encephalopathy, seizures, stroke, or cerebral palsy This chapter is not a comprehensive review of placental pathology; for this the reader is referred to five general references.1–5 Rather, it addresses three topics: (1) the optimal use of the pathology service to obtain useful information; (2) an explanation of specific patterns of placental injury; and (3) clinicopathologic correlation (i.e., which lesions are seen in which clinical situations).
paragraphs.heading: RAYMOND W. REDLINE

paragraphs.text: Because not all placentas are submitted to pathology, every obstetric service should have a specific list of situations in which a placental examination is indicated. Box
paragraphs.heading: Optimal Use of Pathology Service

paragraphs.text: 25.1 provides a list compiled by the College of American Pathologists in collaboration with a panel of neonatologists and obstetricians.6 Because many sick neonates are transported from other hospitals, there should be a policy to ensure a timely placental examination. One solution is to bring the placenta along with the neonate to the tertiary care center. For various reasons, the transport of the tissue specimen itself is sometimes impractical. In these cases, the slides and pathology report from the referring hospital can be requested and reviewed by the pathologist at the hospital where the neonate is to be treated. Whenever possible, placentas should be refrigerated immediately after delivery and sent without fixative to the pathology laboratory. Specimens maintained in this fashion remain useful for at least 7 days after delivery. When refrigeration within 1 to 2 hours of delivery is impossible, placentas should be immersed in 2 to 3 volumes of formalin; placentas can remain in formalin for an indefinite period before examination by the pathologist.
paragraphs.heading: Optimal Use of Pathology Service

paragraphs.text: An informed evaluation of the placenta requires that the pathologist be aware of the clinical situation. Some mechanism, usually a form, must be established to convey this information. A proper balance should be struck between a totally open-ended form and a tedious checklist. Fig. 25.1 is an example of a form used in our institution that may be useful.
paragraphs.heading: Optimal Use of Pathology Service

paragraphs.text: Placental diagnosis requires very few special studies. Bacterial cultures in cases of suspected chorioamnionitis rarely provide useful information beyond that which is available from placental histology and the infant’s blood culture. Fungal stains of the cord and membranes may occasionally be useful for neonatal management. In certain situations a placental karyotype may be important, both to evaluate constitutional chromosomal abnormalities and to exclude chromosomal anomalies confined to placental tissues (confined placental mosaicism) which are found in rare cases of intrauterine fetal demise and idiopathic FGR.7
paragraphs.heading: Optimal Use of Pathology Service

paragraphs.text: At the simplest level, the placenta is nothing more than fetal blood vessels and surrounding connective tissue enveloped
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: by a continuous layer of epithelium known as trophoblast and sitting in a pool of maternal blood called the intervillous space—the latter being continuously filled and drained by maternal uterine arteries and veins (Fig. 25.2). The same unit of structure is recapitulated in an attenuated form in the placental membranes: early in pregnancy the fetal vasculature and maternal intervillous space involute in that portion of the gestational sac destined to become the membranes, leaving a tough shell of fetal connective tissue and the placental trophoblast in contact with the maternal uterus. An
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: understanding of each of these anatomic compartments and their reaction patterns in abnormal pregnancies provides the basis for understanding placental pathology.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Considering the fetal circulation first, the fetal stromalvascular portion of the placenta is supplied by a pair of umbilical arteries and drained by a single umbilical vein. Because there is an arterial anastomosis near the umbilical cord insertion site, the fetus is not handicapped if one of the arteries is occluded or absent (single umbilical artery). The vein is the sole supply of oxygenated placental blood for the fetus. It also has the thinnest wall and is the most susceptible of the three umbilical vessels to collapse upon compression. Large chorionic plate arteries and veins branching off from the umbilical vessels transmit blood through the proximal stem villi to the distal villous units, where gas exchange occurs. Decreased flow secondary to fetal malperfusion of these vessels leads to luminal occlusion (fetal stem vessel obliteration) and involution of the distal vascular bed (avascular villi).8 These changes are global in the placentas of stillborn fetuses and focal in live-born infants with occlusive placental thrombi. Each distal villous unit consists of a central mature intermediate villus and surrounding terminal villi. Mature intermediate villi contain arterioles that
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: directly regulate flow to the distal villous capillary bed. Distal villous capillaries may occasionally rupture, leading to fetomaternal hemorrhage, but an efficient mechanism for villous repair and re-epithelialization usually restricts the amount of lost fetal blood.9
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Adequate perfusion of the maternal uterine-trophoblastic portion of the placenta depends on pregnancy-related increases in maternal intravascular blood volume and decreases in vascular tone. Chronic medical conditions such as renal disease, essential hypertension, and collagen vascular disease can lead to placental malperfusion by interfering with these systemic accommodations to pregnancy.10 To ensure adequate perfusion of the intervillous space, a placental mechanism has evolved for remodeling and enlarging uteroplacental arteries.11 The placental trophoblast grows down the lumen of these vessels, invades the vascular wall, and replaces the smooth muscle layer with a noncontractile layer of fibrinoid matrix. Failure to execute this sequence because of superficial implantation compromises perfusion; leaves the uteroplacental vessels susceptible to spasm, degeneration, and rupture; and plays an important role in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia, abruptio placentae, and some cases of FGR.12
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Intervening between the fetal and maternal circulations is the villous trophoblast. This barrier consists of a syncytial layer of terminally differentiated trophoblast specialized for gas and nutrient exchange (syncytiotrophoblast) derived from a small number of underlying trophoblastic stem cells (villous cytotrophoblast). In late gestation, the syncytiotrophoblast and its basement membrane fuse with the basement membrane of peripheral villous capillaries to form vasculosyncytial membranes that facilitate gas exchange. Term or near-term placentas that lack adequate vasculosyncytial membranes are at increased risk for stillbirth (delayed villous maturation).13 Turnover of villous trophoblast is
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: accomplished via the formation of syncytial knots (also known as syncytial nuclear aggregates) which are later released into the systemic circulation as new trophoblasts are generated. Syncytial knots form in excess of their rate of release into the intervillous circulation in placentas affected by maternal vascular malperfusion, leading to a stereotypical histologic appearance that is easily detectable by placental examination (accelerated villous maturation).14 It is important that maternal blood contacts a nonadhesive surface to prevent activation of the coagulation system. Studies indicate that the anionic phospholipid-binding protein annexin-V plays an important role in preventing the assembly of active coagulation factor complexes on the trophoblast cell membrane.15 Antiphospholipid antibodies have been shown to displace annexin-V from the cell surface, accounting for pathology resembling preeclampsia in some affected pregnancies. Altered anticoagulant mechanisms in the intervillous space may also play a role in a poorly understood placental lesion with a very high recurrence rate known as massive perivillous fibrin deposition (“maternal floor infarction”). This lesion is characterized by an accumulation of fibrin and trophoblast-derived extracellular matrix material that surrounds terminal villi, compromising intervillous circulation and gas exchange (Fig. 25.3A).16
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Although the two circulations are usually distinct, flowrelated trauma can break down the barrier between them, leading to either fetomaternal hemorrhage or the entry of maternal cells into fetal tissues. When maternal inflammatory cells cross the trophoblastic barrier, they can elicit a graft-versus-host–type response against fetal antigens in the villi. This process, known as villitis of unknown etiology (VUE), is discussed in more detail later.
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The final placental compartment is the fluid-filled sac of membranes, which must rupture to allow vaginal delivery. Theoretically, membranes may rupture prematurely for
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: one of two reasons: increased luminal pressure or decreased structural integrity. Increased pressure can be caused by premature contractions, cervical dilation, or polyhydramnios. Structural integrity may be compromised by trauma, inflammatory responses associated with ascending bacterial infection, or ischemic necrosis caused by maternal vascular compromise. The amniotic fluid contained within the sac is predominantly composed of fetal urine, and changes in fluid volume (oligohydramnios or polyhydramnios) often reflect altered fetal fluid balance. For example, maternal vascular malperfusion can lead to fetal hypovolemia, oliguria, and subsequent oligohydramnios.4 Significant oligohydramnios has been associated with umbilical cord compression, limb deformities, and failure of adequate lung growth.17–19
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Placental membranes can also incorporate various exogenous substances suspended in the amniotic fluid, some of which, such as meconium and bacterial cell wall constituents (e.g., lipopolysaccharide), may damage the membranes and the underlying fetal vessels.20,21 Another exogenous substance sometimes found in the membranes is hemosiderin, which can be an indicator of chronic abruption.22
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Muscularized maternal arteries supplying the intervillous space are susceptible to stenosis, occlusion, or rupture. Stenosis leads to maternal vascular malperfusion, which is characterized by low placental weight, increased syncytial knotting, intervillous fibrin deposition, and villous agglutination, particularly in the “watershed zones” between spiral arteries (see Fig. 25.3B).10,23 Total occlusion of these arteries causes villous infarction. Although experimental studies have shown that 20% to 25% of villous parenchyma can be infarcted without acute fetal compromise,2 these studies fail to account for the impaired status of the remaining placenta in these disorders.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Uterine-Trophoblastic Lesions

paragraphs.text: Rupture of the maternal arteries (abruptio placenta) can occasionally occur secondary to trauma, but more commonly represents ischemia-reperfusion injury with secondary dissolution of the injured vascular wall. The common association of abruption with vasoactive drugs such as nicotine, and especially cocaine, is consistent with this pathogenesis.24,25 Because muscular arteries are incompletely remodeled in preeclampsia, abruptio placenta is especially frequent in this disorder. Chronic abruption can also occur and manifests pathologically as organizing marginal blood clots, chorioamniotic hemosiderin deposition, and placental circumvallation.22 Most evidence to date suggests that chronic abruption represents venous rather than arterial hemorrhage.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Uterine-Trophoblastic Lesions

paragraphs.text: Fetal vessels within the umbilical cord are protected from compression by the extracellular matrix, a hydrated gel known as “Wharton’s jelly.” Several processes lessen this protection: decreased hydration caused by maternal vascular
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Stromal-Vascular Lesions

paragraphs.text: malperfusion; torsion owing to excessive coiling; and insertion of the cord vessels into the membranes, leaving them exposed to trauma.26 The critical parameters for deciding whether a putative cord lesion is significant include local injury at the proposed site of occlusion and distal changes reflecting significantly compromised flow.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Stromal-Vascular Lesions

paragraphs.text: Large vessels in the chorionic plate and stem villi may occasionally undergo thrombotic occlusion (fetal vascular malperfusion, segmental type; see Fig. 25.3C).8 Factors predisposing to thrombosis are similar to those reported in other organs, including inflammation (VUE or chorioamnionitis), toxic damage (prolonged meconium exposure), stasis (chronic umbilical cord obstruction, fetal congestive heart failure), inherited predispositions to clotting (protein C and S deficiencies, maternal antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden), hyperviscosity (fetal polycythemia), and specific maternal diseases (e.g., diabetes mellitus, platelet disorders). Villi downstream from the occlusive thrombi are no longer perfused and become avascular and hyalinized. Consequences of fetal vascular malperfusion include a reduction in the size of the fetal vascular bed available for gas exchange, coexistent thromboembolic disease in the fetus, and (in rare cases) fetal consumptive coagulopathy with disseminated intravascular coagulation or thrombocytopenia.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Stromal-Vascular Lesions

paragraphs.text: Fetal arterioles in mature intermediate villi regulate placental resistance to fetal blood flow, the parameter evaluated in clinical pulsed-flow Doppler studies. Obliteration, stenosis, or spasm of these arterioles can have a profound impact on gas exchange.27 These arterioles have been found to be numerically decreased in autosomal trisomies28 and either obliterated or stenosed in patients with severe FGR.27,29 A large proportion of placentas with these fetal arteriolar changes also show clinical and pathologic evidence of maternal vascular malperfusion.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Stromal-Vascular Lesions

paragraphs.text: Fetal capillaries in the terminal villi can sustain microvascular damage leading to leakage of fluid (villous edema) or blood (villous stromal hemorrhage).19,27 Both lesions have been shown to be associated with adverse outcomes in very premature infants.30,31 Frank rupture of these capillaries causes placental intervillous thrombi and, in some cases, hypovolemia, fetal anemia, and a compensatory increase in circulating, nucleated red blood cells (massive fetomaternal hemorrhage).32,33 Finally, the capillary bed of distal villi can expand by adaptive angiogenesis (chorangiosis) in response to hypoxia. Chorangiosis is defined by a significant proportion of terminal villi having 10 or more capillary crosssections and has been associated with VUE, meconium staining, diabetes, and congenital anomalies.34
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Stromal-Vascular Lesions

paragraphs.text: Acute chorioamnionitis is usually caused by ascending infection, cervicovaginal bacteria that either overwhelm normal cervical host defense mechanisms or gain access to the amniotic cavity after rupture of membranes.35 The inflammatory response to bacterial infection is predominantly neutrophilic and generally involves the membranes and chorionic
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: plate but not the chorionic villi. Acute chorioamnionitis is the most common cause of preterm labor.36 However, few delivered infants are septic at birth, attesting to the effectiveness of the placenta as a protective barrier.
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: Histologic features can help determine the duration of infection in chorioamnionitis.35 In the initial stages (<6 hours), maternal neutrophils enter the membranous chorion and underside of the chorionic plate (maternal stage 1). Later, in maternal stage 2, maternal neutrophils infiltrate the entire chorionic plate and the full thickness of the membranes (6–24 hours). A concomitant fetal neutrophilic response, as manifested by transmigration across the fetal vessel walls, begins in the chorionic plate (fetal inflammatory response in chorionic vessels) and the umbilical vein (fetal stage 1) and is followed by involvement of the umbilical arteries (fetal stage 2). Changes that occur later, such as fetal neutrophils infiltrating the umbilical cord stroma (fetal stage 3) and necrosis of the amnion (maternal stage 3), suggest infection of greater than 24 hours’ duration. Finally, perivascular umbilical arcs of calcific debris, glycoprotein, and neovascularization (subnecrotizing funisitis) or a histiocytic component (subacute chorioamnionitis) suggest prolonged infection of days to weeks in duration.37
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: Infants with subnecrotizing funisitis or subacute chorioamnionitis are at increased risk for chronic lung disease. Data suggest that a severe fetal inflammatory response in chorioamnionitis may be a risk factor for severe neonatal morbidities, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia, necrotizing enterocolitis, cranial ultrasound abnormalities, and long-term neurologic impairment.31,38,39
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: The described patterns are typical for most bacteria. Unusual patterns that can suggest specific organisms are neutrophilic exudates involving the villi and intervillous space (suggestive of Listeria monocytogenes)40 and microabscesses on the external surface of the umbilical cord (suggestive of Candida albicans).41
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: Chronic placentitis is caused by hematogenous infection, where organisms enter the placenta via the maternal bloodstream. The hallmark of most cases of chronic placentitis is destructive, diffuse villitis with fibrosis and calcification.4 Although villous inflammation is most common, these infections can also involve the chorion, decidua, and intervillous space. Infectious placentitis is caused by organisms of the so-called TORCH group (Toxoplasma gondii, rubella virus, CMV, and herpes simplex virus), Treponema pallidum, other herpesviruses (Epstein-Barr virus, varicella zoster), and a few selected other organisms, including Zika virus and SARS- CoV-2.42,43 Distinct histopathologic features typify specific etiologic agents (e.g., increased Hofbauer cells, periarteritis, and necrotizing umbilical phlebitis in syphilis; villous plasma cells in CMV; stromal necrosis and calcification in herpes simplex virus; umbilical cord pseudocysts in toxoplasmosis; and diffuse trophoblast necrosis with chronic intervillositis in SARS-CoV-2).
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: Two other categories of neonatal infection that cannot be evaluated directly by placental pathology are transplacental and intrapartum infections. Transplacental infections
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: spread to the fetus without affecting the placenta, presumably through breaks in the interhemal barrier (maternofetal transfusion). Important organisms in this category include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus, human parvovirus B19, and enteroviruses. Intrapartum infections are acquired by the fetus during passage through a contaminated birth canal and spare the placenta. Prominent in this category are venereal pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and human papillomavirus, and some pathogens associated with neonatal sepsis (e.g., group B streptococci and Escherichia coli).
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

paragraphs.text: Foci of idiopathic chronic villous inflammation, VUE, are common in term placentas (5% of all placentas), whereas infectious placentitis is rare (1–2 per 100 live births).28 Certain features of VUE differ from infectious placentitis. VUE is confined to villi and generally involves only a fraction of the villous tree. The predominant cells in VUE are infiltrating T lymphocytes of maternal origin. VUE has a high recurrence risk and tends to occur in older women with previous pregnancies as compared with infectious placentitis, which tends to occur in younger women and rarely recurs because of acquired immunity. For these reasons most experts believe that VUE represents a graft-versus-host– type response related to the genetic differences between the mother and fetus. The chronic villous stromal inflammation associated with VUE causes placental dysfunction by increasing the diffusion distance for gas exchange (see Fig. 25.3D). Data suggest that another closely related graft-versus-host–type reaction, chronic chorioamnionitis, may play a role in some cases of idiopathic preterm labor.44
paragraphs.heading: Inflammatory Lesions, Graft-Versus-Host Type

paragraphs.text: A final group of lesions involves abnormalities in placental structure. As with structural abnormalities in infants, these placental lesions can reflect either primary maldevelopment or secondary deformation and disruption. The uterine decidua is believed to regulate the depth of uterine implantation. Prior surgery or other uterine abnormalities can interfere with normal decidualization, leading to uncontrolled placental growth into or through the uterine wall (placenta accreta spectrum disorders).4 A long-held theory has been that growth abnormalities such as bilobation, accessory lobes, peripheral umbilical cord insertions, and placenta previa develop when the placenta migrates away from uterine defects toward sites with a better maternal blood supply, a process termed trophotropism.1 Other data suggest that these abnormalities may be more closely related to deficient branching of major chorionic vessels and the villous parenchyma they supply.45
paragraphs.heading: Developmental and Structural Lesions

paragraphs.text: Placental structural anomalies can also predict deformations or disruptions in the fetus. Placental amniotic bands are associated with fetal amputations.4 Amnion nodosum, developing secondary to prolonged oligohydramnios, is
paragraphs.heading: Developmental and Structural Lesions

paragraphs.text: associated with pulmonary hypoplasia.19 Placental thrombi can be a harbinger of fetal coagulopathies such as stroke, thrombotic liver disease, renal vein thrombosis, intestinal atresia, or purpura fulminans.4 Placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic diamnionic twins can cause circulatory shifts, leading to acute hypoxic-ischemic injury, or chronic circulatory imbalance, leading to twin-to-twin transfusion and discordant fetal growth.46 Monochorionic monoamnionic twins, although rarely affected by twin-totwin transfusion, commonly have another placental complication—entangled umbilical cords—which can lead to the death of one or both twins.
paragraphs.heading: Developmental and Structural Lesions

paragraphs.text: Abnormal coiling of the umbilical cord is another important structural correlate of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Mechanisms of abnormal coiling are poorly understood but may include early embryonic maldevelopment, dyssynchrony in the growth of vessels, differential blood flow within arteries, and repetitively biased fetal movements.47 Hypocoiling, defined as less than 1 coil/10 cm, has been associated with fetal distress, oligohydramnios, preterm delivery, intrauterine growth restriction, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, fetal heart rate (FHR) alterations, and low cord pH. Hypercoiling (>3 coils/cm) has been associated with constriction of the umbilical vessels (thin cord syndrome), perinatal asphyxia, and intrauterine fetal death.48 Noncoiled umbilical cords are considered a risk factor for poor perinatal outcome and stillbirth.49
paragraphs.heading: Developmental and Structural Lesions

paragraphs.text: Tumors are occasionally found in the placenta. The most common placental tumor is the chorangioma, a benign lesion composed of proliferating fetal blood vessels. Chorangiomas can occasionally cause fetal complications by arteriovenous shunting, leading to hydrops fetalis and platelet sequestration, resulting in disseminated intravascular coagulation.1,4 Choriocarcinomas (malignant trophoblastic tumors) may rarely arise from the villi of second- and third-trimester placentas and occasionally metastasize to the fetus.50 The placenta can also be the site of metastasis for malignant tumors from either the mother (e.g., melanoma, adenocarcinoma) or the fetus (e.g., congenital neuroblastoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis).
paragraphs.heading: Developmental and Structural Lesions

paragraphs.text: The various anatomic, physiologic, and pathologic reaction patterns discussed earlier are placed in clinical context by reviewing their relative frequency in common obstetric and neonatal disease syndromes (Box 25.2).
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: Preterm labor and delivery are most commonly associated with histologic acute chorioamnionitis.36 In many cases, it can be difficult to determine whether infection develops before or after the onset of labor. Because chorioamnionitis generally triggers labor relatively rapidly, most cases that develop after prolonged membrane rupture likely represent secondary infection. Many of the remaining cases of preterm birth fall into three groups: placental abruption, maternal vascular malperfusion, and uterine structural anomalies without associated placental abnormalities (e.g.,
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: so-called cervical insufficiency).51 As mentioned, idiopathic chronic inflammation (chronic chorioamnionitis) also may be implicated in some cases.44
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: FGR can either be constitutional, relating to small maternal size, malnutrition, or an anomalous fetus, or directly caused by placental disease. The most frequent placental causes of FGR are maternal vascular malperfusion and VUE.10,52 Other, less frequent etiologies are fetal vascular malperfusion, massive perivillous fibrin deposition (“maternal floor infarction”), and confined placental chromosomal mosaicism.7
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: Intrauterine fetal demise, particularly at or near term, is often clinically unexplained. Studies suggest that placental examination can reveal the underlying cause or causes in up to 60% to 70% of cases, much more frequently than autopsy.53 One important group at increased risk for stillbirth are fetuses with clinical entanglements or pathologic lesions of the umbilical cord. These lesions can be diagnosed by using specific pathologic criteria.54 Another distinct group at risk are infants whose placentas have decreased vasculosyncytial membranes (delayed villous maturation), leading to decreased placental reserve and susceptibility to transient hypoxic events.13
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: The prototype for this subgroup is the infant of a diabetic mother. A less common but important cause of stillbirth is massive fetomaternal hemorrhage, which is manifested in the placenta by villous edema and increased circulating nucleated red blood cells.32,33 Chronic fetomaternal hemorrhage and its accompanying anemia can cause congestive heart failure and hydrops fetalis. Other forms of hydrops fetalis causing stillbirth that can be identified by placental examination include infections such as human parvovirus B19, toxoplasmosis, and syphilis. Finally, a large proportion of stillbirths is associated with underlying FGR. These cases are characterized pathologically by severe examples of one or more than one of the chronic disease processes discussed earlier.55
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: Central nervous system injury has been associated with several placental lesions. White matter damage, periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, and cerebral palsy in preterm infants have been linked to severe villous edema, chorionic vessel thrombi associated with histologic chorioamnionitis, and multiple placental lesions.31 Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and cerebral palsy in term infants can follow acute birth asphyxia, recurrent intermittent hypoxia, or chronic uteroplacental disease.39 Placental findings associated with birth asphyxia include abruptio placentae, occlusive umbilical cord accidents, and rupture of fetal vessels.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: cular, fetal vascular, inflammatory, and developmental.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Correlation

paragraphs.text: Recurrent intermittent hypoxia is most often related to clinical or pathologic umbilical cord problems and is commonly accompanied by an increase in circulating nucleated red blood cells in the placenta.56 The most common chronic uteroplacental lesions associated with brain injury are those affecting large fetal vessels, including segmental fetal vascular malperfusion, VUE with stem vessel obliteration, severe fetal chorioamnionitis, and meconium-associated vascular necrosis.57 As is true for the preterm group, term infants with multiple placental lesions are also at very high risk.39
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: The placenta is the link that connects the clinical status of the neonate with underlying maternal and fetal disease processes. Careful evaluation of this organ not only provides useful diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic information but also enhances overall understanding of perinatal biology. Communication among neonatologists, obstetricians, and placental pathologists brings together distinct pieces of a puzzle that none can fully solve alone. Through this process, meaningful explanations of the reasons for adverse perinatal outcomes and their chances of recurrence can be provided for concerned physicians and family members.

25 Placental Pathology

### RAYMOND W. REDLINE

The placenta has two opposing functions. It is the sole source of sustenance for the fetus and its sole protection against noxious external influences. It can be argued that no evaluation of a sick neonate is complete without knowing the status of the organ that has accompanied it through the preceding gestation. The specific “value added” by placental examination can be summarized under five overlapping headings: 1. Identification of immediately treatable processes: for

example, elevated risk of neonatal sepsis (histologic chorioamnionitis with fetal inflammatory response), specific infections (cytomegalovirus [CMV], Candida, syphilis, Listeria, SARS-CoV2), retained placenta, metabolic storage diseases, placental malignancies 2. Determination of the underlying cause of adverse out-

comes: subclassification of preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction (FGR), and stillbirth into pathophysiologically homogeneous phenotypes 3. Estimation of recurrence risk: different patterns of pla-

cental injury have distinct and widely disparate rates of recurrence varying from 0% to 70% 4. Guidance for future care path(s): may prompt screening for

underlying maternal disease and/or genetic testing, high-risk referral, enhanced antenatal surveillance, initiation of antenatal therapy, elective early delivery in future pregnancies 5. Quality assurance and risk management: gold standard

distinguishing true and false-positive and negative clinical diagnoses (e.g., chorioamnionitis, abruption); identifies subacute and chronic disorders predisposing to neonatal encephalopathy, seizures, stroke, or cerebral palsy This chapter is not a comprehensive review of placental pathology; for this the reader is referred to five general references.1–5 Rather, it addresses three topics: (1) the optimal use of the pathology service to obtain useful information; (2) an explanation of specific patterns of placental injury; and (3) clinicopathologic correlation (i.e., which lesions are seen in which clinical situations).

### Optimal Use of Pathology Service

Because not all placentas are submitted to pathology, every obstetric service should have a specific list of situations in which a placental examination is indicated. Box

25.1 provides a list compiled by the College of American Pathologists in collaboration with a panel of neonatologists and obstetricians.6 Because many sick neonates are transported from other hospitals, there should be a policy to ensure a timely placental examination. One solution is to bring the placenta along with the neonate to the tertiary care center. For various reasons, the transport of the tissue specimen itself is sometimes impractical. In these cases, the slides and pathology report from the referring hospital can be requested and reviewed by the pathologist at the hospital where the neonate is to be treated. Whenever possible, placentas should be refrigerated immediately after delivery and sent without fixative to the pathology laboratory. Specimens maintained in this fashion remain useful for at least 7 days after delivery. When refrigeration within 1 to 2 hours of delivery is impossible, placentas should be immersed in 2 to 3 volumes of formalin; placentas can remain in formalin for an indefinite period before examination by the pathologist.

An informed evaluation of the placenta requires that the pathologist be aware of the clinical situation. Some mechanism, usually a form, must be established to convey this information. A proper balance should be struck between a totally open-ended form and a tedious checklist. Fig. 25.1 is an example of a form used in our institution that may be useful.

Placental diagnosis requires very few special studies. Bacterial cultures in cases of suspected chorioamnionitis rarely provide useful information beyond that which is available from placental histology and the infant’s blood culture. Fungal stains of the cord and membranes may occasionally be useful for neonatal management. In certain situations a placental karyotype may be important, both to evaluate constitutional chromosomal abnormalities and to exclude chromosomal anomalies confined to placental tissues (confined placental mosaicism) which are found in rare cases of intrauterine fetal demise and idiopathic FGR.7

For example, maternal vascular malperfusion can lead to fetal hypovolemia, oliguria, and subsequent oligohydramnios.4 Significant oligohydramnios has been associated with umbilical cord compression, limb deformities, and failure of adequate lung growth.17–19

Placental membranes can also incorporate various exogenous substances suspended in the amniotic fluid, some of which, such as meconium and bacterial cell wall constituents (e.g., lipopolysaccharide), may damage the membranes and the underlying fetal vessels.20,21 Another exogenous substance sometimes found in the membranes is hemosiderin, which can be an indicator of chronic abruption.22

### Maternal Uterine-Trophoblastic Lesions

Muscularized maternal arteries supplying the intervillous space are susceptible to stenosis, occlusion, or rupture. Stenosis leads to maternal vascular malperfusion, which is characterized by low placental weight, increased syncytial knotting, intervillous fibrin deposition, and villous agglutination, particularly in the “watershed zones” between spiral arteries (see Fig. 25.3B).10,23 Total occlusion of these arteries causes villous infarction. Although experimental studies have shown that 20% to 25% of villous parenchyma can be infarcted without acute fetal compromise,2 these studies fail to account for the impaired status of the remaining placenta in these disorders.

Rupture of the maternal arteries (abruptio placenta) can occasionally occur secondary to trauma, but more commonly represents ischemia-reperfusion injury with secondary dissolution of the injured vascular wall. The common association of abruption with vasoactive drugs such as nicotine, and especially cocaine, is consistent with this pathogenesis.24,25 Because muscular arteries are incompletely remodeled in preeclampsia, abruptio placenta is especially frequent in this disorder. Chronic abruption can also occur and manifests pathologically as organizing marginal blood clots, chorioamniotic hemosiderin deposition, and placental circumvallation.22 Most evidence to date suggests that chronic abruption represents venous rather than arterial hemorrhage.

### Fetal Stromal-Vascular Lesions

Fetal vessels within the umbilical cord are protected from compression by the extracellular matrix, a hydrated gel known as “Wharton’s jelly.” Several processes lessen this protection: decreased hydration caused by maternal vascular

malperfusion; torsion owing to excessive coiling; and insertion of the cord vessels into the membranes, leaving them exposed to trauma.26 The critical parameters for deciding whether a putative cord lesion is significant include local injury at the proposed site of occlusion and distal changes reflecting significantly compromised flow.

Large vessels in the chorionic plate and stem villi may occasionally undergo thrombotic occlusion (fetal vascular malperfusion, segmental type; see Fig. 25.3C).8 Factors predisposing to thrombosis are similar to those reported in other organs, including inflammation (VUE or chorioamnionitis), toxic damage (prolonged meconium exposure), stasis (chronic umbilical cord obstruction, fetal congestive heart failure), inherited predispositions to clotting (protein C and S deficiencies, maternal antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden), hyperviscosity (fetal polycythemia), and specific maternal diseases (e.g., diabetes mellitus, platelet disorders). Villi downstream from the occlusive thrombi are no longer perfused and become avascular and hyalinized. Consequences of fetal vascular malperfusion include a reduction in the size of the fetal vascular bed available for gas exchange, coexistent thromboembolic disease in the fetus, and (in rare cases) fetal consumptive coagulopathy with disseminated intravascular coagulation or thrombocytopenia.

Fetal arterioles in mature intermediate villi regulate placental resistance to fetal blood flow, the parameter evaluated in clinical pulsed-flow Doppler studies. Obliteration, stenosis, or spasm of these arterioles can have a profound impact on gas exchange.27 These arterioles have been found to be numerically decreased in autosomal trisomies28 and either obliterated or stenosed in patients with severe FGR.27,29 A large proportion of placentas with these fetal arteriolar changes also show clinical and pathologic evidence of maternal vascular malperfusion.

Fetal capillaries in the terminal villi can sustain microvascular damage leading to leakage of fluid (villous edema) or blood (villous stromal hemorrhage).19,27 Both lesions have been shown to be associated with adverse outcomes in very premature infants.30,31 Frank rupture of these capillaries causes placental intervillous thrombi and, in some cases, hypovolemia, fetal anemia, and a compensatory increase in circulating, nucleated red blood cells (massive fetomaternal hemorrhage).32,33 Finally, the capillary bed of distal villi can expand by adaptive angiogenesis (chorangiosis) in response to hypoxia. Chorangiosis is defined by a significant proportion of terminal villi having 10 or more capillary crosssections and has been associated with VUE, meconium staining, diabetes, and congenital anomalies.34

### Inflammatory Lesions, Infectious

Acute chorioamnionitis is usually caused by ascending infection, cervicovaginal bacteria that either overwhelm normal cervical host defense mechanisms or gain access to the amniotic cavity after rupture of membranes.35 The inflammatory response to bacterial infection is predominantly neutrophilic and generally involves the membranes and chorionic


## PDF page 444 | printed page 429

plate but not the chorionic villi. Acute chorioamnionitis is the most common cause of preterm labor.36 However, few delivered infants are septic at birth, attesting to the effectiveness of the placenta as a protective barrier.

Histologic features can help determine the duration of infection in chorioamnionitis.35 In the initial stages (<6 hours), maternal neutrophils enter the membranous chorion and underside of the chorionic plate (maternal stage 1). Later, in maternal stage 2, maternal neutrophils infiltrate the entire chorionic plate and the full thickness of the membranes (6–24 hours). A concomitant fetal neutrophilic response, as manifested by transmigration across the fetal vessel walls, begins in the chorionic plate (fetal inflammatory response in chorionic vessels) and the umbilical vein (fetal stage 1) and is followed by involvement of the umbilical arteries (fetal stage 2). Changes that occur later, such as fetal neutrophils infiltrating the umbilical cord stroma (fetal stage 3) and necrosis of the amnion (maternal stage 3), suggest infection of greater than 24 hours’ duration. Finally, perivascular umbilical arcs of calcific debris, glycoprotein, and neovascularization (subnecrotizing funisitis) or a histiocytic component (subacute chorioamnionitis) suggest prolonged infection of days to weeks in duration.37

Infants with subnecrotizing funisitis or subacute chorioamnionitis are at increased risk for chronic lung disease. Data suggest that a severe fetal inflammatory response in chorioamnionitis may be a risk factor for severe neonatal morbidities, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia, necrotizing enterocolitis, cranial ultrasound abnormalities, and long-term neurologic impairment.31,38,39

The described patterns are typical for most bacteria. Unusual patterns that can suggest specific organisms are neutrophilic exudates involving the villi and intervillous space (suggestive of Listeria monocytogenes)40 and microabscesses on the external surface of the umbilical cord (suggestive of Candida albicans).41

Chronic placentitis is caused by hematogenous infection, where organisms enter the placenta via the maternal bloodstream. The hallmark of most cases of chronic placentitis is destructive, diffuse villitis with fibrosis and calcification.4 Although villous inflammation is most common, these infections can also involve the chorion, decidua, and intervillous space. Infectious placentitis is caused by organisms of the so-called TORCH group (Toxoplasma gondii, rubella virus, CMV, and herpes simplex virus), Treponema pallidum, other herpesviruses (Epstein-Barr virus, varicella zoster), and a few selected other organisms, including Zika virus and SARS- CoV-2.42,43 Distinct histopathologic features typify specific etiologic agents (e.g., increased Hofbauer cells, periarteritis, and necrotizing umbilical phlebitis in syphilis; villous plasma cells in CMV; stromal necrosis and calcification in herpes simplex virus; umbilical cord pseudocysts in toxoplasmosis; and diffuse trophoblast necrosis with chronic intervillositis in SARS-CoV-2).

Two other categories of neonatal infection that cannot be evaluated directly by placental pathology are transplacental and intrapartum infections. Transplacental infections

spread to the fetus without affecting the placenta, presumably through breaks in the interhemal barrier (maternofetal transfusion). Important organisms in this category include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus, human parvovirus B19, and enteroviruses. Intrapartum infections are acquired by the fetus during passage through a contaminated birth canal and spare the placenta. Prominent in this category are venereal pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and human papillomavirus, and some pathogens associated with neonatal sepsis (e.g., group B streptococci and Escherichia coli).

### Inflammatory Lesions, Graft-Versus-Host Type

Foci of idiopathic chronic villous inflammation, VUE, are common in term placentas (5% of all placentas), whereas infectious placentitis is rare (1–2 per 100 live births).28 Certain features of VUE differ from infectious placentitis. VUE is confined to villi and generally involves only a fraction of the villous tree. The predominant cells in VUE are infiltrating T lymphocytes of maternal origin. VUE has a high recurrence risk and tends to occur in older women with previous pregnancies as compared with infectious placentitis, which tends to occur in younger women and rarely recurs because of acquired immunity. For these reasons most experts believe that VUE represents a graft-versus-host– type response related to the genetic differences between the mother and fetus. The chronic villous stromal inflammation associated with VUE causes placental dysfunction by increasing the diffusion distance for gas exchange (see Fig. 25.3D). Data suggest that another closely related graft-versus-host–type reaction, chronic chorioamnionitis, may play a role in some cases of idiopathic preterm labor.44

### Developmental and Structural Lesions

A final group of lesions involves abnormalities in placental structure. As with structural abnormalities in infants, these placental lesions can reflect either primary maldevelopment or secondary deformation and disruption. The uterine decidua is believed to regulate the depth of uterine implantation. Prior surgery or other uterine abnormalities can interfere with normal decidualization, leading to uncontrolled placental growth into or through the uterine wall (placenta accreta spectrum disorders).4 A long-held theory has been that growth abnormalities such as bilobation, accessory lobes, peripheral umbilical cord insertions, and placenta previa develop when the placenta migrates away from uterine defects toward sites with a better maternal blood supply, a process termed trophotropism.1 Other data suggest that these abnormalities may be more closely related to deficient branching of major chorionic vessels and the villous parenchyma they supply.45

Placental structural anomalies can also predict deformations or disruptions in the fetus. Placental amniotic bands are associated with fetal amputations.4 Amnion nodosum, developing secondary to prolonged oligohydramnios, is

associated with pulmonary hypoplasia.19 Placental thrombi can be a harbinger of fetal coagulopathies such as stroke, thrombotic liver disease, renal vein thrombosis, intestinal atresia, or purpura fulminans.4 Placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic diamnionic twins can cause circulatory shifts, leading to acute hypoxic-ischemic injury, or chronic circulatory imbalance, leading to twin-to-twin transfusion and discordant fetal growth.46 Monochorionic monoamnionic twins, although rarely affected by twin-totwin transfusion, commonly have another placental complication—entangled umbilical cords—which can lead to the death of one or both twins.

Abnormal coiling of the umbilical cord is another important structural correlate of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Mechanisms of abnormal coiling are poorly understood but may include early embryonic maldevelopment, dyssynchrony in the growth of vessels, differential blood flow within arteries, and repetitively biased fetal movements.47 Hypocoiling, defined as less than 1 coil/10 cm, has been associated with fetal distress, oligohydramnios, preterm delivery, intrauterine growth restriction, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, fetal heart rate (FHR) alterations, and low cord pH. Hypercoiling (>3 coils/cm) has been associated with constriction of the umbilical vessels (thin cord syndrome), perinatal asphyxia, and intrauterine fetal death.48 Noncoiled umbilical cords are considered a risk factor for poor perinatal outcome and stillbirth.49

Tumors are occasionally found in the placenta. The most common placental tumor is the chorangioma, a benign lesion composed of proliferating fetal blood vessels. Chorangiomas can occasionally cause fetal complications by arteriovenous shunting, leading to hydrops fetalis and platelet sequestration, resulting in disseminated intravascular coagulation.1,4 Choriocarcinomas (malignant trophoblastic tumors) may rarely arise from the villi of second- and third-trimester placentas and occasionally metastasize to the fetus.50 The placenta can also be the site of metastasis for malignant tumors from either the mother (e.g., melanoma, adenocarcinoma) or the fetus (e.g., congenital neuroblastoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis).

FGR can either be constitutional, relating to small maternal size, malnutrition, or an anomalous fetus, or directly caused by placental disease. The most frequent placental causes of FGR are maternal vascular malperfusion and VUE.10,52 Other, less frequent etiologies are fetal vascular malperfusion, massive perivillous fibrin deposition (“maternal floor infarction”), and confined placental chromosomal mosaicism.7

Intrauterine fetal demise, particularly at or near term, is often clinically unexplained. Studies suggest that placental examination can reveal the underlying cause or causes in up to 60% to 70% of cases, much more frequently than autopsy.53 One important group at increased risk for stillbirth are fetuses with clinical entanglements or pathologic lesions of the umbilical cord. These lesions can be diagnosed by using specific pathologic criteria.54 Another distinct group at risk are infants whose placentas have decreased vasculosyncytial membranes (delayed villous maturation), leading to decreased placental reserve and susceptibility to transient hypoxic events.13

A less common but important cause of stillbirth is massive fetomaternal hemorrhage, which is manifested in the placenta by villous edema and increased circulating nucleated red blood cells.32,33 Chronic fetomaternal hemorrhage and its accompanying anemia can cause congestive heart failure and hydrops fetalis. Other forms of hydrops fetalis causing stillbirth that can be identified by placental examination include infections such as human parvovirus B19, toxoplasmosis, and syphilis. Finally, a large proportion of stillbirths is associated with underlying FGR. These cases are characterized pathologically by severe examples of one or more than one of the chronic disease processes discussed earlier.55

Central nervous system injury has been associated with several placental lesions. White matter damage, periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, and cerebral palsy in preterm infants have been linked to severe villous edema, chorionic vessel thrombi associated with histologic chorioamnionitis, and multiple placental lesions.31 Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and cerebral palsy in term infants can follow acute birth asphyxia, recurrent intermittent hypoxia, or chronic uteroplacental disease.39 Placental findings associated with birth asphyxia include abruptio placentae, occlusive umbilical cord accidents, and rupture of fetal vessels.

### Summary

The placenta is the link that connects the clinical status of the neonate with underlying maternal and fetal disease processes. Careful evaluation of this organ not only provides useful diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic information but also enhances overall understanding of perinatal biology. Communication among neonatologists, obstetricians, and placental pathologists brings together distinct pieces of a puzzle that none can fully solve alone. Through this process, meaningful explanations of the reasons for adverse perinatal outcomes and their chances of recurrence can be provided for concerned physicians and family members.
